source.title: EuroLLM: Multilingual Language Models for Europe
source.authors: Pedro Henrique Martins; Patrick Fernandes; João Alves; Nuno M. Guerreiro; Ricardo Rei; Duarte M. Alves; José Pombal; M. Amin Farajian; Manuel Faysse; Mateusz Klimaszewski; Pierre Colombo; B. Haddow; José G. C. de Souza; Alexandra Birch; André Martins

record.file_problem: Text appears to contain the full paper; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Applies multilingual scaling-law analysis in a multilingual language-model setting, training model sizes and data-mixture variants and reporting results on held-out domain test sets.
record.gate_note: The scaling-law figures are referenced but their plotted values are not present in the supplied text. The paper reports qualitative outcomes for varying parallel-data proportions and repeated Wikipedia data. It does not report numerical exponents or a validation against much larger runs.
record.test_reason: The paper uses a cited multilingual joint scaling law (Fernandes et al. 2023) only as a tool for choosing its data mix. It fits that law on 100M–341M models and reports qualitative effects of the share of parallel data and of repeating Wikipedia. It does not report whether loss follows a power law, any exponents, any check of predictions against larger runs, any compute-optimal allocation, or downstream scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate about the data-mix decisions. It should add that these led to 20% parallel data per language and to repeating high-quality data. The paper's main conclusion is the release of EuroLLM-1.7B and EuroLLM-1.7B-Instruct, which perform competitively on multilingual benchmarks and machine translation. The authors do not draw conclusions about scaling laws themselves.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts joint scaling-law analysis to multilingual data-mixture choices, varying language-data weights and repetition; it does not reproduce the original broad parameter/token/compute scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary by test domain and data-mixture condition: parallel data benefits parallel test sets, while repeating Wikipedia benefits Wikipedia test sets; parallel-data gains diminish from 25% to 37.5%.

fits_no_version.finding: Under fitted joint multilingual scaling laws (100M–341M models, 100B tokens): adding parallel data does not hurt web or Wikipedia performance and improves parallel-test performance, with diminishing returns from 25% to 37.5%. Repeating Wikipedia helps Wikipedia tests without hurting web tests.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-mixture choices (share of parallel data, repeating high-quality data) shift domain-specific performance in multilingual LLM scaling fits.

record.problems: Scaling-law results are shown only in figures not included in the supplied text; numerical results, fitted exponents, and uncertainty estimates are not stated. The reported domain-test metric is not identified as cross-entropy loss.

untested.parts: No report of fit quality, exponents, or the form of loss versus N, D or C. The fitted curves appear only in figures.
No check of extrapolation to larger runs. The 1.7B model's loss is not compared with predictions.
No scaling-law form is reported for repeated data or other regimes.
Benchmarks are reported only for one model size, against baselines.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling-law fits appear only in Figures 2 and 3. The text gives no numbers, metric or exponents. This is an application of a cited law to choose a data mix, so it is classed as T4 rather than T3.

versions.untested_parts: The supplied text does not identify the reported domain-test metric as cross-entropy loss, and does not test scaling over tokens or compute.
No larger-run validation of predictions fitted on smaller runs is reported.
No loss-minimising parameter/token allocation as a function of compute is tested.
No controlled comparison of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
The experiments concern multilingual text models; no other modality, repeated-data power-law form, fine-tuning scaling law, or transfer scaling law is tested.
Benchmark results are reported, but downstream performance is not tested for predictable scaling with model size or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices, nor evidence of curves bending away from a power law.

relation.reason: The study uses scaling laws to guide its training-data mixture; its reported results do not test any listed claim version.

tranche.reason: Sections 2.2.1–2.2.2 repurpose a cited joint scaling law to choose parallel-data shares and Wikipedia repetition. The reported findings concern data-mixture performance, without evaluating power-law fit, extrapolation accuracy, or compute-optimal allocation.

source_check.notes: All six qualitative findings match the text. Figures 2–3 have no extracted numerical plot values; the Wikipedia-repetition experiment does not explicitly list model sizes.
